newsitem.title: INDIA: Security vigil in India state after leader arrest.
newsitem.headline: Security vigil in India state after leader arrest.

text.p: Authorities in India's second most populous state maintained a strict vigil on Thursday after the arrest of a charismatic politician in a corruption scandal.

Former Bihar chief minister Laloo Prasad Yadav surrendered before a special court on Wednesday and has been ordered held in judicial custody for two weeks while investigators question him in connection with a $280 million farm funds scandal.
Politicians and officials said they saw no immediate threat of violence although supporters of Yadav, a low-caste leader, blocked roads on Wednesday and called a general strike for Friday.
The state capital Patna was quiet on Thursday morning but was patrolled by paramilitary police reinforcements.
Yadav's wife Rabri Devi, an unschooled housewife who was catapulted into the chief minister's job last Friday when Yadav resigned under pressure, appealed for calm.

"It is possible that some self-seeking, communal or feudal elements or those opposed to our policies may try to take advantage of the situation," Devi said in front-page advertisements in Patna's newspapers.
"Keeping in view the political and social challenges facing us, it is imperative that we do not let the situation in the state worsen in any way,..." Devi said.

Bihar is one of India's poorest states and is frequently wracked by violence between lower and upper Hindu castes. Landowners maintain private armies in the resource-rich region where poor roads and communications make lawkeeping difficult.

Yadav's restive supporters said they were keen to help his wife, who was rubber-stamped by lawmakers from Yadav's Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) party and responded by naming more than half the lawmakers to a record-breaking 75-member cabinet.
"This is our government, so workers will not indulge in violence even though there is great resentment among them," said RJD acting president Ranjan Yadav.
Former chief minister Yadav, who has been indicted in the scandal involving the siphoning off of state farm funds, insists he is innocent.
Politicians say peace in the state is crucial for Devi because the federal government could be under pressure to dismiss her rule if law and order breaks down.
Yadav headed Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's Janata Dal party until July 5 when he resigned in a leadership dispute to set up the breakaway RJD group.

India's ruling 15-party United Front coalition has been sharply divided by a debate over corruption and Gujral's failure to take firm action against Yadav, who was first indicted in the farm scandal in April.

The charismatic Yadav, who ruled Bihar for seven years, travelled in a motorcade to court on Wednesday after the Supreme Court rejected his appeal for "anticipatory bail," allowed under Indian law to persons apprehending arrest.

"With typical showmanship, he has converted a moment of humiliation into one of glory, dodging arrest only so that he could stage-manage his surrender," the Times of India said in an editorial on Thursday.
